clauses.t: Patients arrive at a two-room clinic after long drives, often sick, often with a child in tow, and fill in a paper form that asks the same question three ways.
The intake should take the questions to them one at a time, in plain words, on a borrowed tablet
so the nurse gets a history she can trust and the patient feels expected rather than processed.
A volunteer-run library lends drills, ladders and pressure washers, and today the catalogue is a spreadsheet only two people understand.
Design is needed so a neighbour can see what exists, what is out, and how to borrow it without phoning anyone, and so the library feels like a shared shed, not a rental counter.
Grantees spend days each year rewriting the same outcomes into our report template, and we read them looking for two numbers.
The report should ask for what we actually use
show grantees what we did with last year's answers
and make honesty about a failed program feel safe to write down.
Dispatchers juggle forty trucks across three screens and a phone, and the cost of a missed exception is a load sitting at a dock overnight.
The console has to make the one truck that needs attention impossible to miss
and keep the thirty-nine that are fine quietly out of the way.
The shop's character is its staff picks and handwritten shelf cards, and none of that survives on the current site, which looks like every other storefront.
The site should feel like walking in
opinionated recommendations first, events second, the catalogue third
with ordering simple enough that nobody gives up and buys elsewhere.
Residents applying for a fence or a deck permit cannot tell whether their application is moving, so they call the office, and the calls slow the office down.
Design should show every applicant where their permit is, who has it, and what happens next
in language a first-time homeowner understands.
Newcomers want to practise the local language with people, not drills, and local volunteers want to help but do not know where to start.
The app should pair them for short, low-stakes conversations
protect the newcomer's privacy completely
and never make anyone feel graded.
Our audience is ageing and the younger people who do come say the programme reads like a legal notice.
The season should be presented as a set of evenings worth looking forward to, each with a reason to come
while keeping the subscribers who love the composer-and-opus listings.
Reagents expire on shelves because nobody knows who ordered them, and students reorder what is already in the freezer.
The inventory needs to be faster to update than ignoring it
readable from a phone in a glove
and clear about what is dangerous before it is clear about what is cheap.
My grandmother's recipes live on stained index cards in three households, and the cousins argue about which version is real.
The archive should keep every version side by side with who wrote it and when
feel warm rather than clinical
and make it easy for the youngest cousin to add the card she found.
Technicians climb turbines only in safe weather windows, and planning those climbs across a hundred turbines is done on a whiteboard.
Design is needed to show the weather window, the crew and the fault list together
so a planner can commit a day in minutes and a technician knows why they are on that tower.
Our members chose us because we are local and human, and our app feels like it was bought from a vendor, because it was.
The app should do the everyday things fast
and make the human parts visible
a named advisor, plain fees, and a way to talk to someone who knows the member's history.
Visitors carry their phones through the galleries but the current guide asks them to type object numbers and then stare at a screen.
The guide should let people look at the art, not the phone
offering a story when they pause and staying silent when they move on.
New contributors read the docs, fail to build the project, and leave without telling us.
The documentation should get someone from clone to a passing test in one sitting
say plainly what is unfinished
and make the people behind the project visible enough that asking a question feels allowed.
Volunteers sit with dying patients, and a missed shift means someone spends their last afternoon alone.
Scheduling should make coverage gaps obvious to the coordinator days ahead
make swapping a shift easy without guilt
and respect that these volunteers are giving something heavy.
Shoppers wander the market looking for the one stall that sells duck eggs, and vendors move every week.
The map should be the first thing people check on the walk over
show what is in season and who has it today
and give small vendors the same presence as the big ones.
After an outage we write a review document that nobody reads twice, and the same failure returns six months later.
The tool should make the timeline and the decisions easy to reconstruct
keep blame out of the structure itself
and connect each review to the ones before it so patterns surface.
The summer reading programme rewards pages read, and the kids who read slowly quit by July.
The tracker should celebrate showing up and finishing
let a child see their own progress without comparing it to anyone else's
and give parents a reason to visit the library rather than just the app.
Our buildings are quiet and site-specific, and portfolio sites in our field shout with full-bleed renders.
The portfolio should let the work breathe
show the context each building responds to
and read like the studio talks: slowly, precisely, with a point of view a client can disagree with.
Tenants in one building rarely know their neighbours share the same broken boiler and the same unanswered emails.
The hub should make it safe to report a problem
show tenants they are not alone
and turn scattered complaints into a record the union can take to the landlord
without exposing anyone who is afraid.
Readers should be able to stay with a long article without being pulled away.
Most of them arrive tired and on a phone, and if the page fights them they leave.
Use a serif for the body at a large size.
Keep the ads out of the text column.
Frightened people need to find their appointment without having to think.
A missed appointment can cost someone months of treatment.
Big buttons
high contrast everywhere
Nothing should move on the page.
Someone should understand this is worth years of saving before they read a word.
The product has to feel unhurried and rare.
Dark backgrounds with a single gold accent.
Very slow fades between images.
Engineers on call need to see what broke in the first ten seconds.
Every extra click during an outage costs their customers money.
Monospace for all the numbers.
Dense tables separated by thin lines instead of cards.
Build it with server components so it loads fast.
Kids who struggle with reading should finish a page and want the next one.
Their parents need to trust that it is teaching and not just entertaining.
Round corners
bright primary colours
Characters bounce when you get a word right.
People dread this and need to feel they will not make an expensive mistake.
It should remove the fear of getting it wrong, one question at a time.
Show one question per screen
with a progress bar.
Use a calm blue.
Listeners should feel they found something nobody else knows about.
The label exists to keep strange records in print, and the site has to earn that.
Huge condensed type that runs off the edge.
Sharp corners
no shadows.
A person standing at a stop in the rain needs the next bus in one glance.
It has to work for people who do not read the local language.
Line colours match the signs in the stations.
Cache the timetable so it works offline.
Neighbours should know what is fresh today and come in before it sells out.
It should feel warm.
A cream background
with a hand-drawn logo.
Update the menu from a spreadsheet each morning.
Lawyers have to be able to defend every result in front of a judge.
The design needs to prove where each answer came from.
Citations in small caps beside the text.
Two columns with generous margins.
People who have quit before need a reason to come back on a bad day.
Missing a day must not feel like failing.
Celebrate a streak with confetti.
Send a reminder through a push notification at the time they usually train.
Someone new should write correct code without asking anyone.
Maintainers are drowning in the same questions, and the docs have to take that load.
A narrow reading column with a sidebar.
Generate the pages from the source code.
Visitors should leave with a question they cannot stop thinking about.
The objects have to come first and the interface has to disappear.
Lots of empty space around each image.
Quiet transitions
nothing that draws the eye.
Students should always know what they can safely spend this week.
Most of them have never been shown how money works and are embarrassed to ask.
The balance is the biggest thing on the screen.
Make it friendly and modern.
Farmers need to compare machines on their phone between jobs with dirty hands.
A wrong purchase can ruin a season.
Large tap targets
very little text
Load low resolution images first.
Someone in a bad moment should feel less alone within a minute of opening this.
They should never feel judged for what they say.
If they need more help than this can give, they should find it without searching.
Reps waste their mornings hunting for the same three numbers.
A new hire should be useful in their first week.
Nobody should have to ask finance for a report again.
I want black and white with one red accent.
Space Grotesk for the headings.
A big grid of project thumbnails on the home page.
Hover to scale the image up slightly.
Use the new purple as the primary colour.
Round everything to 8 pixels.
Add a soft shadow to every card.
Roll it out through a shared component library.
It should be clean and modern.
Make the checkout flow three steps.
Sticky header with the event name.
Use a 4 pixel spacing grid.
